output.title: Design against untested assumptions by narrowing one workflow
output.body:
If you want to design against untested assumptions, start by narrowing the decision. Don’t ask, “Can AI do this?” Ask, “Which one recurring workflow is repetitive, measurable, and already lives in digital tools and English-language documents?”

That question matters because the demo version of a task can hide the hard part. In a live workflow, the real assumptions are usually about data quality, approval steps, and how much handover work sits around the task. If those parts are unclear, the system is not ready for a build, even if the idea looks neat on paper.

For a small business owner, the practical test is simple: write down the one workflow, how often it happens, what outcome you can observe, and where human approval must stay in place. Money movement and other high-risk decisions stay human. That is not a limitation; it is the control.

Bareni’s position is to work inside the customer’s environment, hand over finished code, and keep database, automation-tool, and API accounts in the customer’s name from the start. That is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

The next step is to make the assumption list explicit before you build anything. If the workflow cannot be named clearly, it is probably too fuzzy to automate yet.
